title: As if today (I.23)
hookLine: act in each thing as if you were to die today
tomorrow: how do you change without burning out by week two?

cards: Last practice before a move. Last shift before someone retires. Last dinner with everyone home before somebody leaves for college.
People act differently on a last time. They say the thank-you. They take the photo.
They don't spend the hour on their phone. Nobody has to tell them to. The Imitation asks for that kind of attention on ordinary days, and its reason is blunt.
In the morning, it says, consider that you may not reach evening; in the evening, don't promise yourself the morning.

teach.b: Chapter twenty-three of book one is about death, and it's gentler than its subject. Practical, not morbid. Today a person is here, it says; tomorrow, gone, and once out of sight, soon out of mind.

teach.h: AS IF YOU WERE TO DIE TODAY.
teach.b: Then the line the day is named for: in every act and every thought, order yourself as if you were to die today. Notice what it doesn't ask for. Not fear.
If your conscience were clear, the book says, you wouldn't fear death much; it's better to avoid sin than to run from death.
And it gives a practical warning: don't leave to friends and family, after you're gone, what you can do for your own soul now.

teach.h: DO GOOD WHILE YOU HAVE TIME.
teach.b: Do good while you have time. One more line, and it's the kindest. The chapter calls happy the person who keeps the hour of death before their eyes and gets ready for it every day.

But ready doesn't mean packing a bag. In this chapter it means not leaving the apology for later, or the call, or the kindness. Some people hear a line like this and think: you only live once, so go wild.

The Imitation means nearly the opposite. Not recklessness, and not gloom. It's last-practice attention, turned on an ordinary Tuesday: the next conversation, the next chore, done as if nothing came after it.

how: Many Catholics examine their conscience each night, and the Church prays for a holy death; the Imitation's chapter on death is read as a call to live each day well rather than to fear.

o: act carefully so that nothing ever goes wrong
live each act as if this were your last day
live for the moment and forget the future

games.q: morning and evening — tap the pairs.

s: as if today means live recklessly, since you only live once
the Imitation means a clear conscience and full attention now, not going wild.
the chapter says a clear conscience makes death less fearful
with a good conscience, it says, you wouldn't fear death much.
the Imitation tells readers to fear death above all
it says it's better to avoid sin than to run from death.

games.q: your grandfather starts the story you've heard many times, at a busy family dinner. what does chapter twenty-three point toward?
o: listen to it fully, as if it might be the last telling.
politely remind him that he's told it before.
check your phone until he gets to the end.
games.why: the chapter says order each act as if you were to die today, and do good while you have time. full attention is the good here.

practice: Bring to mind one message you've been putting off: a thank-you, an apology, a plain I'm proud of you. Write it now, in simple words, as if there won't be a better time, and hold it until the sit ends. Short is fine.
If you pray, you can offer the person to God as you write.

wordCard.voice: As if today. The Imitation's counsel: order each act and each thought as if this were the last day, with a clear conscience.

orig.note: Latin: remember you will die; a phrase for the kind of reflection the Imitation's chapter on death practices (not a phrase from the chapter itself).

carryVoice: Keep this one: as if today, since tomorrow isn't promised and today is right here. See you soon.
